ai.title: Mammary Duct Ectasia
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Mammary duct ectasia is a benign, inflammatory dilation of subareolar ducts causing nipple discharge and periductal fibrosis. It mimics infection or carcinoma, especially in low‑resource settings where imaging is limited.

b: Benign, self‑limiting in most cases
Often bilateral, but may be unilateral
Associated with nipple retraction and green‑yellow discharge
sections.p: Duct ectasia occurs when the terminal lactiferous ducts near the nipple become dilated, filled with secretions, and inflamed. It is most common in perimenopausal women but can appear at any age.

b: Obstruction → stasis → inflammation → fibrosis
Plasma‑cell rich infiltrate distinguishes it from acute bacterial mastitis
Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hormonal changes, local trauma
sections.p: The pathology is periductal fibrosis with plasma‑cell infiltrate. The obstruction leads to stasis, secondary infection, and possible ulceration of the nipple.

b: Discharge may be painless or mildly tender
Nipple retraction suggests chronic fibrosis
Absence of systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis) points away from acute infection
sections.p: Patients present with a sticky, often greenish discharge, nipple crusting, and sometimes a palpable subareolar mass. The main challenge is differentiating it from carcinoma or abscess, especially where ultrasound or mammography are unavailable.

t.b: Distinguishes solid mass from cystic dilated ducts; a hypoechoic tubular structure supports ectasia
Cytology to exclude malignancy; presence of benign epithelial cells and plasma cells supports ectasia
Shows dilated ducts without suspicious microcalcifications

b: Ask about duration, colour, and amount of discharge
Inspect for nipple inversion or ulceration
Palpate for a firm, non‑fluctuant subareolar mass
sections.p: Focus on history of discharge, nipple changes, and risk factors. Physical exam should assess for a subareolar induration, retraction, and any signs of infection.

b: Warm compresses and gentle nipple hygiene
Topical corticosteroid cream to reduce inflammation
If secondary bacterial infection suspected, use a narrow‑spectrum oral antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin) – avoid broad‑spectrum agents unless culture‑guided
Surgical excision of the affected duct (microdochectomy) for persistent symptoms
sections.p: Treat conservatively; address inflammation, prevent secondary infection, and monitor for malignant change.

b: Breast carcinoma (especially Paget disease)
Acute bacterial mastitis/abscess
Intraductal papilloma
sections.p: Conditions that cause nipple discharge or subareolar masses can be mistaken for duct ectasia.

b: A clean‑looking discharge does not exclude malignancy
Absence of systemic signs does not rule out a secondary abscess
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, normal ultrasound may be falsely reassuring if the operator lacks experience; discharge cytology can miss low‑grade carcinoma.
